\chapter{One to Five — Where the Character Is the Count}
\label{ch:zh-numbers}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to five in Mandarin and read all five characters cold and out of order, and I know which of them I could have worked out and which I simply had to learn.}

The five numerals read out of sequence, then off a lift panel with the fourth floor missing — and the reader knows why it is missing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[yī]{\zh{一} — one stroke, and that is the character}

\label{lesson:ZH-W03-yi}



\begin{quote}
Two chapters ago a character was a block to take apart. You learned pieces first, then the characters they build. This chapter asks nothing of the sort. Put the pieces down.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the whole character}
Here it is:

\begin{quote}
\zh{一}
\end{quote}

That is not a fragment. \textbf{That is the character.} One horizontal stroke, drawn left to right across the middle of the square, and nothing else.

Write it: \textbf{one héng stroke, left to right.} No pen lifts, because there is nothing to lift between. It is the shortest character you will ever write.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{一} — one stroke, left to right, straight and level
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A character you did not have to decompose. How many times did you lift the pen? (\textbf{Not once}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yī]{\zh{一} — one, and the number is the strokes}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-yi}



\begin{quote}
Draw the shape you just learned. One stroke, left to right.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{一}} \emph{yī} means \textbf{one}.

Read those two facts together, because their meeting is the point:

\textbf{One stroke. And it means one.}

Chinese will do this exactly three times, and you are about to meet all three in a row. It is the gentlest corner of a writing system with a reputation for being anything but.

Now the sound, and here is something new. Every word this book has given you so far has dipped (\emph{nǐ}, \emph{hǎo}, \emph{ěr}) or risen (\emph{rén}). This one does neither.

\textbf{First tone: high and flat.} Start high and stay there — not a question, not a statement, just a held note. Hum a single steady pitch and put \emph{yi} on it. \emph{Twice through:}

One honest note, so it does not surprise you later. \textbf{\zh{一} does not always keep this tone.} In front of certain syllables it shifts to \emph{yí} or \emph{yì} — the same kind of change that turned \zh{你好} into \emph{ní hǎo}. Counting is exactly where it stays \emph{yī}, so counting is where this book leaves it.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yī} — high and flat, held
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{一} — say it, then say how many strokes it has
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which tone is \emph{yī} — the dipping one, or the flat one? (\textbf{Flat}, held high.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[èr]{\zh{二} — two bars, and neither is decoration}

\label{lesson:ZH-W03-er}



\begin{quote}
Draw the character for one. Now guess what two looks like before you read on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — you were right}
\begin{quote}
\zh{二}
\end{quote}

Two strokes, both horizontal, and the order is the one this book has repeated since the person radical: \textbf{top before bottom.}

But look properly, because they are \textbf{not the same length}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{upper} bar is the \textbf{shorter} one
  \item the \textbf{lower} bar is the \textbf{longer} one
\end{itemize}

That is not decoration. A character occupies a square, and two identical bars floating in one look like an accident. The widening bottom gives the block a base to sit on. You will meet the same instinct everywhere: the last horizontal tends to be the widest, because it is the one holding everything up.

Write it: \textbf{short bar. Lift. Long bar beneath.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{二} — short bar on top, then the long one below
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two strokes for two. Which goes first? (The \textbf{top}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[èr]{\zh{二} — two, and a syllable you have met before}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-er}



\begin{quote}
Draw the shape. Two bars, short over long. Count the strokes and say what number you expect it to be.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{二}} \emph{èr} means \textbf{two}. Two strokes, and it means two — the pattern holds.

\textbf{èr} is \textbf{fourth tone}, the last of the four you had not used in a real word. Fourth tone \textbf{falls}, sharply and from a height, the way an English speaker says a short firm \emph{\textquotedblleft{}No.\textquotedblright{}} Drop it, do not trail it. {[}REPEAT x2{]}

Now hold \textbf{èr} next to a piece you already know:

\begin{quote}
\zh{尔} \emph{ěr} — the sound-component inside \zh{你}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\zh{二} \emph{èr} — the number two
\end{quote}

\textbf{Same syllable. Different tone. Completely unrelated characters.} One dips; one falls. Nothing else separates them.

You met this idea once already, when \zh{好} \emph{hǎo} \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} turned into \zh{好} \emph{hào} \textquotedblleft{}fond of\textquotedblright{} on a change of pitch alone. That was one character with two readings; this is two characters colliding in sound. Both are the same lesson: \textbf{in Mandarin the pitch is not decoration on the word. It is part of the word.}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{èr} — falling, dropped firmly
  \item \textbf{ěr}, then \textbf{èr} — dip, then fall. Feel the difference in your throat.
  \item \textbf{yī, èr} — flat, then down
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \emph{ěr} from \emph{èr}? (\textbf{Only the tone} — and they are different characters entirely.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sān]{\zh{三} — three bars, and the pattern's last stand}

\label{lesson:ZH-W03-san}



\begin{quote}
One bar. Two bars. Say what comes next out loud before you look.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the pattern holds one last time}
\begin{quote}
\zh{三}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Three strokes.} Top, then middle, then bottom — the same rule, a third time.

The lengths are not a simple ladder:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{top} bar is medium
  \item the \textbf{middle} bar is the \textbf{shortest} of the three
  \item the \textbf{bottom} bar is by far the \textbf{longest}
\end{itemize}

Pinching the middle and widening the base keeps \zh{三} from reading as three identical lines you would have to stop and count. Your eye takes it in whole. That is the difference between a \textbf{character} and a \textbf{tally} — and the reason the next one cannot be four bars.

Write it: \textbf{top, lift, middle, lift, bottom.} Two pen lifts.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{三} — top, middle short, bottom long
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} — point at each and count its strokes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Imagine four bars stacked in a square. Could you read it, or would you have to \textbf{count} it? (Count it — which is why the next character is not four bars.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sān]{\zh{三} — three, and the end of the easy road}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-san}



\begin{quote}
Draw the three bars. Middle short, bottom long.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{三}} \emph{sān} means \textbf{three}. Three strokes, three — for the third and last time.

\textbf{sān} is \textbf{first tone}, the flat high one you met on \emph{yī}. Hold it level. The \emph{a} is open, the \emph{n} light at the end. {[}REPEAT x2{]}

So of your first three numbers, two sit flat and one falls:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{yī} flat, \textbf{èr} falling, \textbf{sān} flat
\end{quote}

Say the run. It goes \emph{level, down, level}, and that shape is the first thing a listener recognises — before any of the individual words.
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
Three characters in, one stroke per unit, a system so regular it barely needs teaching. \textbf{It stops here}, and you should know why before it happens.

Every counting system humans have built hits the same wall in the same place. Roman numerals go I, II, III and then break to IV, because stacked marks stop being readable at about three. This one breaks for exactly the same reason.

You are being told now so that the next character feels like a solved problem rather than a broken promise.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yī, èr, sān} — level, down, level
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} — say each as you point at it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Three characters, three stroke counts, nothing memorised. That ends now.

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sì]{\zh{四} — a box, and the rule that governs every box}

\label{lesson:ZH-W03-si}



\begin{quote}
Draw one, two and three. You were told this is where it stops.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — five strokes, for four}
\begin{quote}
\zh{四}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Five strokes, for the number four.} The trick is gone, exactly as promised.

\zh{四} is a \textbf{box with two things inside it}, and every box obeys one rule: \textbf{close the bottom LAST.} Walls, then contents, then shut the door.

In order:

1. the \textbf{left vertical}, top to bottom 2. the \textbf{top and right side in one turning stroke} — across, then down without lifting the pen at the corner 3. the short \textbf{inner left-falling} stroke 4. the \textbf{inner stroke that turns up} at its foot 5. the \textbf{bottom bar}, closing the box — \textbf{last}

Two strokes of wall, two of filling, one to shut the door. Four pen lifts.

Notice that the corner in step 2 is \textbf{one stroke, not two.} A horizontal that turns and runs downward without the pen leaving the paper is a single unit — \emph{héngzhé}, \textquotedblleft{}horizontal-turn\textquotedblright{}. Miscounting it is the commonest way a beginner's stroke count goes wrong.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{四} — walls, then the two inner strokes, then the bottom last
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the turning corner one stroke or two? (\textbf{One} — \emph{héngzhé}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sì]{\zh{四} — four, borrowed for its sound}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-si}



\begin{quote}
Draw the box. Walls, contents, bottom last. Count the strokes: five, for the number four.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{四}} \emph{sì} means \textbf{four}, and the shape has nothing to do with fourness.

\zh{四} is not a picture of four things. It is a shape that already meant something else, \textbf{borrowed for its sound} — the same move you met in \zh{尔}, a piece carried for how it sounds rather than what it means. The borrowing won outright: nobody reads \zh{四} as anything but four now.

\textbf{sì} is \textbf{fourth tone}, falling, like \emph{èr}. The vowel is not the \emph{ee} of \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{}: after \emph{s}, pinyin \emph{i} is a tight buzz in the same position as the \emph{s} itself. Say \emph{sss}, then voice it without moving your tongue. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
A reason to get that tone right, and it is a real one:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{sì} (falling) — four
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{sǐ} (dipping) — die
\end{quote}

Separated \textbf{by pitch alone} — the third time this chapter has shown you that tone is part of a Mandarin word's identity, not an accent on it.

Not a curiosity, either: it is why many buildings in China number floors 1, 2, 3, 5, skipping four the way some Western buildings skip thirteen.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{sì} — falling, firm
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{四} — in order, then out of order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Four is the first number here you could not work out. What replaced the trick? (\textbf{A shape borrowed for its sound}, built to a rule.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǔ]{\zh{五} — count the strokes and be wrong}

\label{lesson:ZH-W03-wu}



\begin{quote}
Guess, out loud, how many strokes the character for five will have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — four, for five}
\begin{quote}
\zh{五}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Four strokes. For five.}

If you guessed five, good — that guess is the point. The trick that carried you through the first three is not merely retired, it now actively misleads.

The four strokes, in order:

1. the \textbf{top horizontal}, left to right 2. the \textbf{descending stroke}, from the top bar down, leaning slightly left 3. the \textbf{turning stroke} — across to the right, then down 4. the \textbf{bottom horizontal}, the widest in the character, closing it

You already know why the last is widest: it is the base, the same instinct as the long bottom bar of \zh{二} and \zh{三}. Three pen lifts.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{五} — top bar, descender, turn, then the wide base
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{四} \zh{五} — name each shape without saying the numbers yet
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke is widest, and why? (The \textbf{bottom} — it is the base.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wǔ]{\zh{五} — five, and the run is complete}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-wu}



\begin{quote}
Draw the shape. Four strokes — for five.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{五}} \emph{wǔ} means \textbf{five}.

\textbf{wǔ} is \textbf{third tone}, the low dipping one you have had since \emph{nǐ}. Keep it low and let it creak; do not push it back up. {[}REPEAT x2{]}

You already own two words on this tone:

\begin{quote}
\zh{你} \emph{nǐ}, \zh{好} \emph{hǎo}, \zh{五} \emph{wǔ}
\end{quote}

All three dip. Say them in a row: the pitch should not change shape once, only the mouth around it.

One spelling note while you are here. In \emph{wǔ} there is no consonant hiding under that \textbf{w}: the \emph{w} \textbf{is} the \emph{u}, written that way because pinyin does not begin a syllable with a bare \emph{u}. Round your lips and voice it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — one to five}]
You can now count:

\begin{quote}
\zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{四} \zh{五}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{yī, èr, sān, sì, wǔ}
\end{quote}

Say it as one run, not five separate words. The tone shape is \textbf{level, down, level, down, dip}, and that rhythm is what a listener hears first.

Five characters, and three ways one can come to you: two you derived, one was borrowed for its sound, and two you simply learned. That mix is Chinese writing in miniature, and you have now met all of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{nǐ}, \textbf{hǎo}, \textbf{wǔ} — three dips, one shape
  \item \textbf{yī èr sān sì wǔ} — one run, at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which tone do \emph{nǐ}, \emph{hǎo} and \emph{wǔ} share? (The \textbf{third} — low and dipping.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — read the numbers off a wall}

\label{lesson:ZH-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count to five aloud, in order, without looking. Then do it again with your eyes on the characters:

\begin{quote}
\zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{四} \zh{五}
\end{quote}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the same five, shuffled}
Counting in order is slightly dishonest: the sequence carries you, and you can recite \emph{yī èr sān} without reading anything.

So here they are shuffled. Name each before moving on, without letting your eye run back to the row above:

\begin{quote}
\zh{四} \zh{一} \zh{五} \zh{二} \zh{三}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\zh{三} \zh{五} \zh{一} \zh{四} \zh{二}
\end{quote}

If one of them made you pause, it will be \zh{四} or \zh{五} — the two you could not derive. That is expected, and it tells you exactly which two to drill.

\begin{culture}
Not a party trick. A lift panel, a floor directory, a bus number, a market price — all use these characters \textbf{on their own}, with no sentence around them. That is why five are already useful; you are not waiting on grammar:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{You see:} \zh{三}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{You say:} \emph{sān} — third floor.
\end{quote}

And when the panel reads

\begin{quote}
\zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{五}
\end{quote}

with no \zh{四} between three and five, you know why, and you are not confused by it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Two voices, using only what this book has given you:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{你好} — \emph{ní hǎo} (the sandhi tone, as always)
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{你好} — \emph{ní hǎo}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} {[}pointing at a panel{]} \zh{五} — \emph{wǔ}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{五} — \emph{wǔ}
\end{quote}

Small, and entirely real: repeating a floor number back is what people do in a lift, in any language.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{四} \zh{一} \zh{五} \zh{二} \zh{三} — cover the row above first
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{yī èr sān sì wǔ} — one run, level, down, level, down, dip
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{五} — top bar, descender, turn, wide base
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Five characters, and three different ways a character can come to you:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三}} — transparent. The strokes \emph{are} the number.
  \item \textbf{\zh{四}} — borrowed for its sound, and built on a box whose rule you can reuse.
  \item \textbf{\zh{五}} — plain. Four strokes for five, learned as a shape.
\end{itemize}

That spread is not an accident of this chapter. It is the whole writing system in small: a little of it can be reasoned out, more of it is borrowed sound, and the rest is simply known. You have now met all three, on characters short enough that none of them hurt.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You can read the five characters cold, in any order, with no sentence around them. A panel reads \zh{一} \zh{二} \zh{三} \zh{五} — which number is missing, and why? (\textbf{\zh{四}}, because \emph{sì} sits one tone from \emph{sǐ}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
